What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What do EMT and EMS stand for?
Emergency medical technician and emergency medical services.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why assess airway patency, ventilation, and oxygenation separately?
An open airway can coexist with poor ventilation, and adequate ventilation can coexist with poor oxygenation. Assess early and reassess with change.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What airway competency does Chapter 10 identify from the National EMS Education Standards?
Apply respiratory anatomy and physiology to establish a patent airway, adequate ventilation, and respiration.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What do O₂, CO₂, and ATP stand for in respiratory physiology?
Oxygen, carbon dioxide, and adenosine triphosphate.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is respiration?
Gas exchange at the lungs and tissues and cellular use of oxygen during metabolism.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is pulmonary ventilation?
Mechanical movement of air into and out of the lungs by pressure changes. Also called breathing.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is external respiration?
Exchange between alveoli and pulmonary capillaries. Oxygen moves into blood and carbon dioxide moves into alveoli.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is internal respiration?
Exchange between systemic capillaries and cells. Oxygen moves into cells and carbon dioxide moves into blood.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is cellular respiration and metabolism?
Aerobic metabolism breaks down glucose with oxygen to make ATP, releasing carbon dioxide and water.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How does inhaled oxygen reach body cells?
It enters alveoli, diffuses into pulmonary capillaries, and travels through arteries, arterioles, and systemic capillaries to cells.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How is oxygen transported in blood?
Most binds to hemoglobin inside red blood cells. A small fraction dissolves in plasma.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How does carbon dioxide get from cells to the lungs?
It diffuses into systemic capillaries and returns in venous blood for exhalation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What do oxygenated and deoxygenated mean?
Relatively high and relatively low oxygen content, respectively.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What structures define the upper airway?
Nose and mouth through the larynx to the cricoid cartilage.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What structures define the lower airway?
Trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What do the nasal passages do to incoming air?
Warm, moisten, and filter it across damp mucous membranes. Oral breathing provides less warming and filtration.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Where are the adenoids, uvula, and palate in the upper-airway illustration?
The adenoids are in the nasopharyngeal region. The hard and soft palates separate the mouth from the nasal region, and the uvula hangs from the soft palate.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is a mucous membrane?
A thin tissue lining found on structures such as the nasal passages.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What are the three levels of nasal turbinates?
Superior, middle, and inferior.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What are the three divisions of the pharynx?
Nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx, also called the hypopharynx.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Where is the nasopharynx?
Behind the nasal cavity down to the soft palate.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Where is the oropharynx?
Behind the mouth between the soft palate and epiglottis. It contains the tongue.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What structures are highlighted at the laryngopharynx in the airway illustration?
Vallecula and epiglottis.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why is the pharynx a shared passage?
Air passes toward the anterior trachea, and swallowed material passes into the posterior esophagus to reach the stomach.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is the epiglottis?
A leaf-shaped cartilage behind the tongue that covers the laryngeal opening during swallowing and opens during breathing.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why may manual airway positioning help an unresponsive patient even if no object is visible?
The relaxed tongue or epiglottis can block airflow behind the mouth. Jaw thrust or head-tilt, chin-lift can relieve soft-tissue obstruction.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Where is the larynx, and what is its role?
Between pharynx and trachea. It houses vocal cords for speech and lower-airway protection.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Which anterior laryngeal cartilage is the Adam’s apple?
Thyroid cartilage.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What identifies the cricoid cartilage?
It is the lowermost part of the larynx, immediately below the thyroid cartilage, and the only complete cartilaginous ring of the upper airway.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What airway structures lie anterior and posterior at the lower pharyngeal transition?
The trachea is anterior and the esophagus is posterior. The upper-airway illustration also identifies the thyroid gland near the lower larynx and trachea.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Which membrane lies between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages?
Cricothyroid membrane.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What additional structures are labeled in the front and rear larynx illustrations?
Hyoid and lesser cornu, extrinsic ligament, ventricular fold, arytenoid cartilage, pyriform fossae, cricothyroid ligament, and upper tracheal cartilages.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is the trachea?
The windpipe extending from the larynx to the carina.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How is the tracheal wall supported?
Anterior C-shaped cartilage rings and a flexible posterior smooth-muscle wall. The inner layers include lamina propria and respiratory epithelium.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is the carina?
The point where the trachea divides into the right and left mainstem bronchi.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How do bronchi differ structurally from bronchioles?
Mainstem bronchi contain cartilage. Smaller bronchioles have smooth muscle and a mucous lining without cartilage.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How can asthma progress from airway narrowing to respiratory failure?
Bronchial smooth-muscle constriction and mucosal swelling raise resistance and work of breathing until muscles fatigue and ventilation fails.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What are alveoli?
Tiny air sacs at the ends of bronchioles, surrounded by pulmonary capillaries for gas exchange.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What are the two layers of the pleura?
Visceral pleura covers the lung. Parietal pleura lines the chest wall.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is the pleural space?
The negative-pressure space between the pleural layers. Serous fluid lubricates their motion and helps maintain the seal.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why can air entering the pleural space collapse the lung?
It disrupts the negative-pressure seal, allowing elastic lung tissue to recoil inward.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is the diaphragm and what share of normal ventilatory effort does the chapter attribute to it?
The major, dome-shaped breathing muscle between chest and abdomen. About 60–70%.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What are intercostal muscles?
Muscles between the ribs.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How does active inhalation draw air in?
The diaphragm contracts downward and external intercostals move the ribs and sternum up and out. Thoracic volume increases and lung pressure falls.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What baseline atmospheric pressure is used in the chapter’s ventilation example?
760 mmHg.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What pressures illustrate inspiration in the chapter?
Intrapleural pressure 754 mmHg and intrapulmonary pressure 757 mmHg, below the 760 mmHg atmospheric baseline.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How does normal passive exhalation move air out?
Inspiratory muscles relax, the lungs recoil, and thoracic volume falls, raising lung pressure above atmospheric pressure.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What pressures illustrate expiration in the chapter?
Intrapleural pressure 758 mmHg and intrapulmonary pressure 763 mmHg.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why can exhalation require active effort in obstructive disease?
Air trapping and impaired recoil can require expiratory muscle contraction, increasing fatigue.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Which brainstem centers control breathing rhythm?
Dorsal respiratory group (DRG), ventral respiratory group (VRG), and pontine or pneumotaxic respiratory center.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What do chemoreceptors do in breathing control?
Sense oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH-related changes and adjust respiratory rate and depth.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Where are central chemoreceptors and what drives their response?
In the medulla. Rising CO₂ and related pH changes increase rate and depth.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Where are peripheral chemoreceptors, and what is their key oxygen stimulus?
Carotid bodies and aortic arch. Low arterial oxygen stimulates ventilation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why should the chapter’s hypoxic-drive explanation for COPD be treated cautiously?
A fall in drive can contribute, but excess oxygen can raise CO₂ through other mechanisms, including worsened matching of ventilation and blood flow. It can happen during prehospital care.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is the BLS principle for treating hypoxemia in COPD?
Correct hypoxemia promptly, titrate oxygen per protocol, and assist ventilation if breathing is inadequate.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is oxygenation?
The process of oxygen loading the blood and reaching cells by diffusion.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How do hypoxemia and hypoxia differ?
Hypoxemia conventionally means low arterial oxygen tension. Hypoxia means inadequate oxygen at tissues.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why can anemia or carbon monoxide exposure impair oxygen delivery despite preserved arterial oxygen tension?
Both can reduce usable oxygen carried in the blood. Tissue delivery also depends on perfusion.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What do V/Q and CNS stand for in respiratory assessment?
V/Q is ventilation-to-perfusion matching in the lungs. CNS is central nervous system.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What mechanisms commonly produce low arterial oxygen tension in this chapter?
Inadequate ventilatory drive and mismatching of lung ventilation and perfusion can lower arterial oxygen tension.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is hypoperfusion or shock?
Inadequate delivery of oxygen and nutrients to tissues because perfusion is inadequate, resulting in cellular and organ dysfunction.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What can cause tissue hypoxia?
Airway obstruction, inadequate ventilation, shock, toxic gases, lung disease, CNS depression, stroke, or chest or head trauma.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What breathing and circulatory changes can accompany early hypoxia?
Tachypnea, dyspnea, tachycardia, elevated blood pressure, and pale, cool, clammy skin.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why can skin become pale, cool, and clammy early in hypoxia?
Sympathetic vasoconstriction shunts blood centrally, and sweat glands activate.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What early neurologic findings may accompany hypoxia and rising CO₂?
Restlessness, agitation, headache, disorientation, and confusion.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is cyanosis in a respiratory assessment?
A late blue-gray discoloration of mucosa or skin associated with poor oxygenation or perfusion.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Where should cyanosis be checked?
Oral mucosa, conjunctiva, lips, circumoral skin, and nail beds. Emphasize oral mucosa and conjunctiva in darker skin.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why can cyanosis be absent in severe bleeding or anemia?
Too little hemoglobin may be present to produce visible blue-gray discoloration.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How can cardiac findings progress in severe hypoxia?
Tachycardia can progress to dysrhythmias and bradycardia. Newborn bradycardia, such as a rate below 100/min, can be an early sign.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What neurologic findings suggest severe hypoxia?
Severe confusion, slowed reactions, poor coordination, altered consciousness, or seizures.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is hypercarbia and what findings may accompany it?
CO₂ buildup. Sleepiness, drooping eyelids, and head bobbing upward on inhale and downward on exhale may occur.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What happens to cellular metabolism when oxygen supply is impaired?
Anaerobic metabolism yields less ATP, with lactic acid accumulation, dysfunction, and possible cell death.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How can neurologic disorders disrupt mechanical ventilation?
Brain injury, CNS depressants, or neuromuscular disease impair diaphragm and intercostal activation or strength.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How can injury compromise the chest’s bellows action?
Rib pain, flail chest, diaphragm rupture, and chest compression can restrict effective chest expansion.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What processes can block airway patency?
Edema from infection, allergy, or burns, trauma, a foreign body, or loss of muscle tone.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What can impair alveolar gas exchange?
Fluid or damaged alveoli in pneumonia, edema, drowning, or emphysema. Emphysema-related air trapping also increases fatigue.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What sources impair available oxygen, oxygen transport, or cellular use?
Low ambient oxygen, enclosed fires or toxic exposures, carbon monoxide affecting transport, and cyanide affecting utilization.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What problems can impair oxygen delivery through poor flow or reduced carrying capacity?
Pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, heart failure, tamponade, hypovolemia, or anemia.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why is a blocked nose important in an infant?
Infants rely heavily on nasal breathing and have narrow passages that occlude easily.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Which pediatric airway features predispose to obstruction?
Proportionally large tongue, high U-shaped epiglottis, narrow airway, and easily kinked trachea.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why place padding beneath an infant’s shoulders and upper back when supine?
The large occiput can flex the neck forward. Padding helps restore neutral alignment.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What traditional pediatric airway teaching does the chapter give about the cricoid cartilage?
It describes the less rigid cricoid as the narrowest region in children under 10. Treat this as a textbook anatomic simplification and use device- and age-specific sizing guidance.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why should BVM breaths be gentle in infants and children?
A compliant chest wall can rise easily, and excess tidal volume can overdistend alveoli and injure lungs.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why can children become hypoxic rapidly?
Smaller oxygen reserves and high metabolic demand, described as about twice adult demand in the chapter.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is the chapter’s most common cause of pediatric cardiac arrest?
Hypoxia.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What older-adult changes can make airway positioning and ventilation harder?
Dentition problems, reduced neck mobility, oropharyngeal tumors, and loss of muscle around the mouth that weakens the mask seal.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why are older adults vulnerable to early desaturation and aspiration?
COPD, sleep apnea, and reduced functional residual volume reduce reserve. Gastroesophageal reflux increases aspiration risk, and confusion can limit cooperation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What determines whether an EMT may perform an airway intervention?
State law and licensure set scope. Training, credentialing, agency protocols, and medical direction govern individual authorization.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How do evidence, model guidelines, and local EMS protocols differ?
Studies supply evidence, recommendations interpret it, model guidelines inform systems, and local protocols direct care under physician medical direction.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is a patent airway?
An open airway clear of obstruction.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What findings suggest an open airway in a responsive patient?
Air is heard or felt, speech is in full sentences or near normal, and the voice sounds normal for the patient.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why can an open airway still be unprotected?
Reduced consciousness impairs swallowing, gagging, or coughing. Emesis, pooled secretions, or swelling can cause aspiration or recur even when air currently moves.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What should you reassess in a patient with an open airway who repeatedly needs jaw support?
How quickly snoring returns after release and whether emesis, secretions, or swelling threatens continued airway patency.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is aspiration?
Entry of material such as fluid, blood, food, or vomit into the lungs.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Can a patient with an intact gag or cough still aspirate?
Yes, especially with altered mental status.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How can spontaneous inspiratory effort worsen soft-tissue airway obstruction?
Negative pressure draws relaxed tongue or epiglottic tissue into the airway.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How can facial burns and soft-tissue trauma threaten airway patency?
Burns may cause progressive swelling. Injured tissue and blood around the mouth or jaw can obstruct.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What does snoring suggest in a patient with reduced consciousness?
Partial upper-airway blockage by tongue or pharyngeal tissue. Open the airway and note whether the snoring returns when support is released.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What does crowing indicate?
Spasm around the larynx narrowing the tracheal opening.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What does gurgling indicate and what is the immediate response?
Liquid in the airway, such as blood, secretions, or vomit. Suction promptly.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What does harsh, high-pitched inspiratory stridor suggest?
Significant upper-airway narrowing from laryngeal swelling or a mechanical obstruction.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What clues besides abnormal sounds suggest a blocked airway?
Inability to speak while awake, visible material, and swelling of the tongue, mouth, or oropharynx.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How is the crossed-fingers technique performed?
From above or behind the head, place the crossed thumb on lower incisors and index finger on upper incisors, then open with a scissor motion.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: When is a finger sweep appropriate?
Only to remove a visible solid object. Blind sweeps can push it deeper. Be prepared for biting, gagging, or vomiting.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: If suction is unavailable and no spinal injury is suspected, how can oral liquids be cleared?
Turn the patient to the side and wipe accessible fluid with gauze or a cloth around the index and middle fingers.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What are the three categories of BLS airway-opening or maintenance techniques?
Manual positioning, suction, and oral or nasal adjuncts.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What must be done before applying BVM breaths?
Establish airway patency. Promptly suction obvious obstructing fluids.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: When is head-tilt, chin-lift the initial maneuver?
When spinal injury is not suspected, such as nontraumatic unresponsiveness, apnea, or arrest.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How do you perform an adult head-tilt, chin-lift?
With the patient supine, press the forehead back and lift up and forward under the bony mandible, keeping the mouth slightly open as needed.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why avoid pressing soft tissue under the chin during the chin lift?
It can push tissue into the airway and obstruct airflow.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How should dentures be managed while opening the airway?
Leave stable full dentures in place to preserve mask seal. Remove very loose or dislodged dentures and loose partial plates. Recheck during care.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How can an infant’s sniffing alignment be judged?
The ear opening and sternal notch are horizontally aligned, with gentle positioning and no overextension.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How is head-tilt, chin-lift modified for a child?
Tilt only slightly back from neutral, lifting the bony chin with one index finger without pressing soft tissue.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How can alignment be improved in a larger adult whose chest sits higher than the ears?
Ramp the head and upper torso with blankets or towels until the ear and sternal notch align.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: When is jaw thrust indicated?
Suspected spinal injury, or when head-tilt, chin-lift has failed in a patient without suspected spinal injury.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How is an adult jaw thrust performed?
From the head, brace your elbows and lift both angles of the jaw up and forward, maintaining neutral in-line alignment if spinal injury is suspected. Retract the lower lip if needed.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How is a jaw thrust adapted for an infant?
Support the cheekbones with thumbs and lift the jaw angles using two or three fingers of each hand without compressing soft tissue or tilting the neck.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What should you do if a jaw thrust does not maintain patency?
Reposition the jaw and consider an indicated adjunct. During cardiac arrest, if jaw thrust fails to open the airway, prioritize ventilation and use head-tilt, chin-lift as needed.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: When is a modified lateral recovery position appropriate?
Altered consciousness with aspiration risk, adequate breathing, no need for PPV, and no suspected spinal injury.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How do you position a patient in the modified lateral recovery position?
Set the near arm at a right angle, roll onto the side, support the cheek with the upper hand, and bend the upper hip and knee.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why keep a recovery-position patient lateral and avoid prone positioning?
Lateral positioning lets fluids drain and avoids pressure on the chest. Prone positioning can restrict diaphragm movement.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What recovery-position timing does the chapter specify?
Change sides at 30 minutes or sooner if blood flow to the dependent extremity appears impaired.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How can fluids be drained if spinal injury is suspected?
Maintain spine motion restriction and log roll as a unit when required to drain. Return to supine for BLS mask ventilation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: When should an EMT suction the airway?
Promptly when gurgling occurs or blood, vomitus, secretions, or other liquids obstruct the airway.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is the limitation of suction for solid objects or thick vomit?
A solid object may not pass through the catheter. Drain when safe and remove visible solids only. A hand-powered unit may handle heavier material better.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What PPE does the chapter specify for airway suction?
Gloves, protective eyewear, and a mask. Use an appropriate respirator when airborne precautions are indicated, such as suspected TB or COVID-19.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What performance does the chapter specify for mounted suction?
More than 40 L/min at the tubing end and a vacuum magnitude greater than 300 mmHg with tubing occluded. It must be adjustable for pediatric use.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What vacuum can the chapter’s portable suction device generate?
About 80–120 mmHg of vacuum for pharyngeal suction and 300 mmHg when clamped in the equipment test.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What powers mounted or portable suction?
Mounted devices can use an electric pump or vehicle vacuum. Portable units may be battery, oxygen, or hand powered.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What failure should you anticipate with oxygen-powered or electric portable suction?
Oxygen-powered suction stops when gas runs out. Electric units need charged batteries. Inspect before service and keep backup available.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What supplies should be present with a suction unit?
Wide-bore thick-walled nonkinking tubing, unbreakable collection vessel, rinse water, suitable catheters, and adequate adjustable vacuum and flow.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What are other names for the rigid suction catheter?
Hard catheter, Yankauer, tonsil tip, or tonsil sucker.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Where is a rigid suction catheter used?
Mouth and oropharynx, particularly for particulate material. Advance only as far as visible, generally to the base of the tongue or less.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How does the chapter measure a rigid oral suction catheter?
Angle of jaw to corner of mouth. An illustration also uses corner of mouth to earlobe as an oral landmark.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is a French suction catheter and when is it used?
A soft flexible catheter for the nose and nasopharynx, or when a rigid catheter cannot be used.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How is a soft suction catheter measured for nasal versus oral use?
Nasal tip to ear tip for nasal use and corner of mouth to ear tip for oral use. Avoid advancing past the tongue base during oral suction.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why avoid touching the posterior airway with a suction catheter?
It can cause gagging, vomiting, tissue injury, or vagal bradycardia, especially in children.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Which vacuum pressures does the chapter list for oral suction?
Adult 100–120 mmHg, child 80–100 mmHg, infant 60–80 mmHg. Use the lowest effective vacuum and follow device and agency guidance.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What nasal suction range and backup device does the chapter describe?
A soft catheter at about 80–120 mmHg is the general example, with age-appropriate adjustment. A bulb syringe can be used if a soft catheter is unavailable.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How do you insert and withdraw an oral suction catheter?
Verify assembly, turn on the unit, measure, then insert above the tongue without suction when possible. Apply suction while withdrawing side to side, covering the control port if present.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How can you prevent suction tubing from clogging?
Rinse the catheter and tubing with water as needed.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What time limits does the chapter give for an oral suction pass?
Up to 15 seconds for adults and 3–5 seconds for infants or children. Minimize time without oxygenation or ventilation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What should an EMT do if an adult develops a marked rate or rhythm change while being suctioned?
Stop suction and restore ventilation and oxygenation. The textbook illustrates resuming PPV for at least 30 seconds, subject to local guidance and clinical response.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is residual volume?
Air remaining in the lungs after maximal exhalation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why may oxygen saturation fall during suction?
Suction interrupts airflow, oxygenation, or ventilation. The chapter flags its residual-volume explanation as requiring verification.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What should you do if the heart rate drops during suction?
Stop suction, remove the catheter, give oxygen, and be ready to assist ventilation. Monitor pulse, heart rate, and SpO₂.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How should you interpret the chapter’s prolonged preoxygenation and timed suction cycles?
They are textbook examples. Clear immediately obstructing material promptly, minimize interruption, and use local airway- and device-specific guidance.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What historical timing examples does the chapter show for froth and preoxygenation before suction?
It illustrates adult cycles of 15 seconds suction and 2 minutes oxygenated PPV for persistent froth, and 5 minutes of preoxygenation at 10–12 breaths/min for small secretions. Follow current local guidance for timing.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What can airway adjuncts accomplish and what limitation do they share?
They help maintain patency after opening and clearing the airway. They stop short of the larynx and provide no aspiration protection.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What care continues after placing an OPA or NPA?
Maintain manual positioning, ensure the device is clear, and monitor responsiveness and tolerance. Remove if gagging or increased responsiveness makes it intolerable.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is an OPA?
Oropharyngeal or oral airway. A rigid curved device with a flange that holds the tongue away from the posterior airway and allows suction access.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Who can safely tolerate an OPA according to the chapter?
A completely unresponsive patient without a gag or cough reflex. An intact reflex can lead to vomiting or laryngospasm.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What happens if an OPA is too long or improperly inserted?
An overly long OPA may push the epiglottis over the laryngeal opening. Incorrect insertion can push the tongue posteriorly.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How is an adult OPA sized?
Front teeth to jaw angle or mouth corner to tragus. Source illustrations also show the earlobe or angle of jaw as outer landmarks.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How is an adult OPA inserted using rotation?
Open the mouth, aim the tip toward the palate, and rotate 180° when the tip reaches the soft palate while advancing to seat the flange. A side insertion may use a 90° turn.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How is an OPA sized and inserted in children?
Size from mouth corner to jaw angle in the pediatric example. Use a tongue depressor and advance in normal orientation without rotation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How is an OPA withdrawn when a patient gags?
Pull gently out and down and prepare to manage vomiting.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is an NPA?
Nasopharyngeal or nasal airway. A soft curved hollow tube with a proximal flange and a beveled distal end reaching behind the tongue.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: When may an NPA help?
When the mouth cannot be opened easily or an OPA is poorly tolerated because of an intact gag reflex, if nasal insertion is safe.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: When should an NPA be avoided in trauma?
Suspected basilar skull fracture, severe facial or midface trauma, and possible head trauma in the pediatric section.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What are risks of NPA insertion?
Pain, nasal injury and bleeding, gagging, vomiting, and laryngospasm.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How do you size an NPA?
Measure nose tip to earlobe or jaw angle. Select a diameter that fits without blanching the nostril.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How is an NPA inserted?
Lubricate with sterile water-soluble lubricant, select the more patent nostril, and advance gently along the nasal floor near midline with bevel toward septum or floor until the flange rests at the nostril.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What do you do if an NPA meets persistent resistance or no air moves through it?
Avoid forcing it. If gentle rotation does not help or airflow remains absent in a spontaneously breathing patient, remove and try the other side.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why are NPAs generally avoided in very young children?
The narrow tube can add resistance or clog, and enlarged adenoids can compress the tube or be injured and bleed.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is respiratory rate?
Number of breaths per minute. One inspiration and expiration together count as one breath.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is tidal volume?
The volume of air moved in one breath.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is minute ventilation and how is it calculated?
Air moved per minute: tidal volume × respiratory rate. The chapter gives about 5–8 L/min for a healthy resting adult.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is alveolar ventilation and how is it calculated per minute?
Air reaching alveoli for gas exchange: (tidal volume − dead-space volume) × respiratory rate.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is dead air space and how large is it in an average adult?
Conducting airway volume without gas exchange, about 150 mL. It fills first during each breath.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: At 12 breaths/min and 200 mL tidal volume, what is minute volume?
2,400 mL/min or 2.4 L/min.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: At 12 breaths/min, 200 mL tidal volume, and 150 mL dead space, what is alveolar ventilation?
600 mL/min or 0.6 L/min. Only 50 mL per breath reaches alveoli.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: At 42 breaths/min and 200 mL tidal volume, what is minute volume?
8,400 mL/min or 8.4 L/min.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: At 42 breaths/min, 200 mL tidal volume, and 150 mL dead space, what is alveolar ventilation?
2,100 mL/min or 2.1 L/min. A high minute volume can mask inadequate alveolar ventilation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What does hypopnea mean in the chapter’s assisted-breathing examples?
Shallow breaths with inadequate tidal volume. It can occur even when the respiratory rate is adequate.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What does hypoventilation mean in the chapter?
Ventilation is reduced. Breaths may be too slow, shallow, or both, limiting alveolar air delivery and CO₂ removal.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why can a drop in tidal volume reduce gas exchange so quickly?
The fixed dead-space volume takes up a larger fraction of each breath, leaving disproportionately less air for alveoli.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: When does a rising rate increase useful alveolar ventilation?
When effective depth is maintained. At extremes, shortened filling time can reduce tidal volume and gas exchange.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What two components must be adequate for effective breathing?
Both respiratory rate and tidal volume. This is the chapter’s rule of two.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is the rule of one for inadequate breathing?
Either inadequate rate or inadequate tidal volume is enough to require assisted ventilation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is the treatment distinction between respiratory distress and respiratory failure?
Distress means increased work with adequate ventilation, so give oxygen when indicated and reassess. Failure requires prompt assisted ventilation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why may an oxygen mask fail to help shallow respirations?
Each tiny breath may fill mainly dead space, so little enriched gas reaches alveoli without PPV.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why can SpO₂ improve despite ineffective ventilation?
Oxygen can raise hemoglobin saturation while shallow or slow breathing still fails to remove CO₂.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What four parameters describe breathing?
Rate, rhythm, quality, and depth.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How does the chapter recommend counting a respiratory rate?
Count complete breaths over one full minute.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What do you inspect in the look phase of breathing assessment?
Chest excursion and symmetry, retractions, neck muscle strain, nasal flaring, rhythm, posture, and general distress.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What can speech reveal about breathing?
Short phrases with pauses for air indicate greater respiratory effort. Full sentences with a normal voice support adequate airflow.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How do you assess exhaled volume in an unresponsive patient?
Observe chest rise while listening and feeling for airflow at the nose and mouth with your ear and cheek nearby.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Where are the anterior upper lung auscultation landmarks?
Second intercostal spaces at the midclavicular lines, roughly 2 inches below the clavicles in the chapter illustration.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Where are the lateral and lower anterior lung auscultation landmarks?
Fourth or fifth intercostal spaces along the anterior or midaxillary lines and fifth intercostal spaces beside the sternum.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How should breath sounds be compared?
Listen to a full inhalation and exhalation at matching locations bilaterally, meaning on both sides.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What comes before auscultation in the initial breathing check?
Inspect chest rise and listen and feel for airflow. Auscultation follows as the assessment allows.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What are normal breathing rhythm, quality, and depth?
Regular intervals and consistent volume aside from occasional sighs, full symmetric chest rise and breath sounds, and adequate exhaled flow without excessive muscle use.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What resting respiratory rates does the chapter list for adults and adolescents aged 12–15?
12–20 breaths/min.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What resting respiratory rate does the chapter list for older adults?
About 20–24 breaths/min.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What resting respiratory rate does the chapter list for school-age children aged 6–11?
18–25 breaths/min.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What resting respiratory rate does the chapter list for preschoolers aged 3–5?
20–28 breaths/min.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What resting respiratory rate does the chapter list for toddlers aged 1–2?
22–37 breaths/min.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What resting respiratory rate does the chapter list for infants aged 1–12 months?
30–53 breaths/min.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What resting respiratory rate does the chapter list from birth to 1 month?
40–60 breaths/min.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Which adult respiratory rates does the chapter flag for special concern?
Less than 8 or greater than 24 breaths/min. Interpret rate with effort, depth, and the rest of the exam.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: At what very fast rates does the chapter flag impaired filling time?
Around 40 breaths/min or more in adults and above 60/min in pediatrics. Verify actual depth and air movement.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: A responsive adult after an MVC is upset and breathing at 28/min, but speaks normally with full chest rise and no hypoxia. Is PPV indicated by the rate alone?
No. Assess depth, oxygenation, perfusion, and changes rather than using tachypnea alone.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: An adult has 14–16 breaths/min, slight chest rise, minimal felt airflow, and diminished bilateral sounds. What is needed?
Immediate PPV for inadequate tidal volume despite an apparently normal rate.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: An adult has deep breaths but breathes only 6/min. How should breathing be managed?
Provide immediate PPV because the rate is inadequate despite good depth.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What adult resting rate does the chapter consider elevated even below its 24/min concern threshold?
Above 20/min in a nonstimulated adult, with a separate older-adult resting range. Elevated rate alone does not establish failure.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What do tachypnea and bradypnea mean?
Faster-than-normal and slower-than-normal breathing for the patient’s age and situation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why is bradypnea especially ominous in children?
It can indicate decompensation and inadequate oxygenation. In adults consider CNS depression, including drug or alcohol exposure.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Which neurologic or systemic problems may cause irregular breathing?
Head injury, stroke, severe medical illness, metabolic disturbance, and toxic inhalation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What are retractions and where are they visible?
Inspiratory tissue depressions due to accessory muscle effort, seen between ribs, above clavicles, near the neck or sternum, or below ribs.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What are common visible signs of increased respiratory effort?
Nasal flaring, retractions, diaphoresis, prominent rib contours, open mouth, strained sternocleidomastoids, and tripod posture.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How does normal pediatric abdominal movement differ from seesaw breathing?
Children normally show more abdominal movement. Seesaw breathing means the chest and abdomen move in opposite directions and is concerning.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why does excessive abdominal effort matter during expiration?
It may reflect active use of abdominal muscles to push the diaphragm up and force air out. Compare with normal age-related abdominal movement.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What abnormal sounds may be heard on chest auscultation?
Wheeze, crackles, rhonchi, diminished or absent sounds, and unequal sounds.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What does unequal air entry suggest in an injured or ill patient?
Consider trauma, pneumothorax, infection, or another cause of asymmetric ventilation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is paradoxical chest-wall motion?
A segment moves inward during inspiration and outward during expiration. Also check for splinting and asymmetry.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What defines respiratory failure versus respiratory arrest?
Failure is inadequate rate and/or volume. Arrest, or apnea, is complete cessation of breathing.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What are common causes of respiratory failure or arrest in the chapter?
Stroke, myocardial infarction, opioids or other CNS depressants, toxic inhalation, electrocution or lightning, suffocation, trauma, epiglottic infection, and foreign-body obstruction.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Which organs are especially sensitive to hypoxia and when can brain injury begin?
Brain, heart, and liver. The chapter estimates brain cells begin to die after about 4–6 minutes without adequate oxygen.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What are agonal respirations?
Infrequent, irregular gasps that do not ventilate effectively and may occur near or during arrest.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is the BLS response to unresponsiveness with gasping or absent breathing?
Check for a definite pulse within 10 seconds. Start CPR and use an AED promptly if no definite pulse is felt. With a definite pulse, ventilate and reassess.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why does lower effort after severe distress sometimes indicate deterioration?
A patient who becomes quiet, drowsy, and shallow with poor air entry may be tiring, even if SpO₂ improves on oxygen.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: A patient progresses from pursed lips to tripoding to losing the ability to follow commands with poor chest rise. What changes in BLS care?
Reassess rate and depth throughout. Move from indicated oxygen during adequate ventilation to two-person BVM when ventilation becomes ineffective.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: An unresponsive adult develops snoring and 5–6 shallow breaths/min after a sudden severe headache. What are the immediate BLS priorities?
Open and maintain the airway, assist ventilation with oxygen, and reassess. The history suggests a possible intracranial emergency.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What assessment details despite normal skin color indicate severe compromise in the sudden-headache case?
Unresponsiveness with flexion posturing, snoring, minimal chest rise, 5–6 breaths/min, and SpO₂ 79%. A strong radial pulse near 50/min confirms circulation is present.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What should be reported for sudden severe headache followed by posturing and respiratory failure?
Last known well, onset, neurologic progression, anticoagulants if known, baseline and repeat vitals, and response to ventilation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What does PPV mean and when is it needed?
Positive pressure ventilation forces air into the lungs when breathing is inadequate or absent.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Which basic methods can deliver PPV?
Pocket-mask breaths, one- or two-person BVM, and an automatic transport ventilator where authorized.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How does spontaneous inhalation differ from PPV?
Chest expansion creates negative pressure during spontaneous inhalation. PPV pushes air in and can support ventilation when chest-wall injury impairs expansion.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What airway-wall effect distinguishes PPV from spontaneous breathing in the chapter?
Positive pressure can expand conducting airways and increase the volume of dead space. Judge effectiveness by chest rise and air movement, avoiding excess volume.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How does PPV affect venous return and perfusion?
Higher intrathoracic pressure reduces venous return and can lower preload, stroke volume, blood pressure, and organ perfusion.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: When is the circulatory effect of PPV especially concerning?
Cardiac arrest, low circulating volume, severe air trapping, or tension pneumothorax. Compare pressure, pulse, perfusion, chest rise, and sounds with baseline.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What three capabilities should a mask ventilation device provide?
Tight seal, sufficient lung inflation, and simultaneous supplemental oxygen connection.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What PPE does the chapter specify for ventilating a patient?
Gloves and eye protection, a face mask for heavy contamination, and an appropriate respirator when airborne precautions apply.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is the practical rule for interruptions in ventilation?
Keep interruptions as brief as possible. The chapter’s 30-second ceiling is an older upper limit, not a target.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: For an adult with a pulse and abnormal or absent breathing, what rescue-breathing rate does the chapter’s 2025 AHA update give?
10 breaths/min, or one every 6 seconds.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: For an infant or child with a pulse and inadequate breathing, what rescue-breathing rate does the chapter’s 2025 update give?
20–30 breaths/min, or one every 2–3 seconds.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: When does the chapter’s separate neonatal resuscitation rate of 30–60 inflations/min apply?
When initial PPV is indicated under the resuscitation-at-birth algorithm. An age label alone does not establish that the birth algorithm applies.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What do CPR and AED stand for?
Cardiopulmonary resuscitation and automated external defibrillator.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What adult CPR compression-to-breath ratio and rate does the chapter list for BLS mask ventilation?
30:2 for one or two rescuers, with 100–120 compressions/min.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What infant and child CPR ratios does the chapter list for BLS mask ventilation?
30:2 with one rescuer or 15:2 with two rescuers, with 100–120 compressions/min.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What compression-to-ventilation ratio does the chapter describe for resuscitation at birth?
3:1, corresponding to 90 compressions and 30 ventilations per minute when neonatal compressions are indicated.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Which older ventilation rates are superseded by the chapter’s BLS updates?
Older pulse-present tables list 10–12/min for adults and 12–20/min for infants and children, with a later pediatric example of 20–25/min. The chapter’s 2025 update specifies 10/min for adults and 20–30/min for infants and children with a pulse and inadequate breathing.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How long should a typical BLS assisted breath take?
About 1 second, with enough volume for visible chest rise and time for exhalation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What adult and pediatric delivered volumes does the textbook use as estimates?
Adult example about 10 mL/kg or 700–1,000 mL. Pediatric example about 6–8 mL/kg. In BLS, use visible chest rise and current age- and situation-specific guidance.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What should happen if oxygen is unavailable while a patient needs PPV?
Start effective ventilation with room air and connect supplemental oxygen as soon as practicable.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Which findings suggest effective PPV?
Visible rise and fall with each breath, adequate rate, improving color, and heart rate trending toward normal if other problems do not prevent it.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why might the chest fail to rise during PPV?
Poor seal, inadequate delivered volume, airway obstruction, or device problems.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What does failure of the chest to fall between assisted breaths suggest?
Exhalation is blocked or inadequate because of position, obstruction, device problems, or excessively fast breaths.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What heart rate trend suggests worsening hypoxia during ventilation?
Persistent or worsening tachycardia, or slowing that proceeds to bradycardia. Consider bleeding, anxiety, and cardiac causes as well.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is gastric distention during PPV?
Inflation of the stomach when excessive pressure from fast or large breaths forces air into the esophagus.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How can gastric distention worsen ventilation and oxygenation?
It limits diaphragm excursion, especially in children. Regurgitation and aspiration can cause pneumonia and impair gas exchange.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How do slow, limited breaths reduce gastric inflation?
They limit airway pressure. Deliver over about 1 second and stop at visible chest rise.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why can mouth-to-mouth ventilation supply some oxygen?
The chapter estimates 21% oxygen in room air and about 16% in exhaled air.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: When is mouth-to-mouth or mouth-to-nose considered in the chapter?
When a BVM or pocket mask is unavailable, using a barrier. Mouth-to-nose may help when the mouth cannot be opened or sealed, with severe mouth injury, or in infants as appropriate.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How do you prevent leaks during mouth-to-mouth or mouth-to-nose breathing?
Pinch the nose for mouth-to-mouth and close the mouth for mouth-to-nose.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What features and parts should a pocket mask have?
Transparent mask with a tight seal, ventilation chimney, one-way valve, oxygen inlet, and appropriate adult, child, or infant size.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What are the benefits of a pocket mask compared with one-person BVM?
A single rescuer can use both hands for seal and jaw lift. The barrier and valve reduce exposure, and a better seal can improve volume.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What are limitations of pocket-mask ventilation?
Rescuer fatigue, exposure concerns, and lower achievable oxygen concentration than a BVM with oxygen and reservoir.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How is a pocket mask set up and positioned?
Attach its one-way valve and oxygen tubing at the chapter’s 15 L/min example. Seat the narrow end over the nose bridge and the broad end in the cleft above the chin.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is the difference between cephalic and lateral pocket-mask positioning?
From the head gives a clear view of chest rise. From the side helps a solo rescuer alternate breaths and compressions, but a two-handed seal is harder.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How does the C-E grip open the airway and seal the mask?
Thumb and index finger form a C over the mask. The other three fingers form an E under the mandible and lift the jaw to the mask.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How does the pocket-mask C-E technique change with suspected spinal injury?
Use jaw thrust and neutral in-line alignment. In cardiac arrest, if jaw thrust fails, use the head positioning necessary to ventilate.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What should you check first if a pocket-mask breath produces no rise?
Reposition the airway and retry, then check the mask seal, obstruction, equipment and indicated adjuncts. Follow the current obstruction algorithm if appropriate.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What does BVM stand for and how does it work?
Bag-valve-mask. Squeezing a self-inflating bag drives gas through a nonrebreathing valve and a mask or compatible airway connection.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What are the main components of a BVM?
Mask, exhalation port, nonrebreather valve, self-inflating bag, air/oxygen intake valve, oxygen inlet/tubing, and reservoir.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What oxygen concentration can a BVM deliver with and without supplemental oxygen in the chapter?
About 21% on room air and close to 100% with a reservoir and oxygen at 15 L/min, depending on seal and device.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why choose a BVM by size without using full bag capacity as breath volume?
The bag’s labeled capacity is its maximum, while the patient's delivered breath should produce visible chest rise without overinflation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Which BVM capacities and age cutoffs are given as textbook examples?
Adult bag about 1,600 mL with the older age-8 example. Pediatric bags about 450–500 mL, but the chapter also lists a conflicting neonatal maximum of 250 mL. Verify age- and device-specific sizing.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What BVM equipment specifications does the chapter describe?
Self-refilling bag, nonjamming nonrebreather valve rated up to 30 L/min, oxygen inlet and reservoir, standard 15/22-mm fittings, transparent masks, and equipment suited to operating temperatures. Follow device instructions for any pressure-relief valve.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How do you select a BVM mask that fits?
It spans the bridge of the nose to the cleft below the lower lip and allows a seal without soft-tissue pressure under the chin.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How are roles divided in preferred two-person BVM ventilation?
One rescuer positions the airway and seals the mask with both hands. The other squeezes the bag steadily to visible chest rise.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How does a lone rescuer perform BVM ventilation?
Use the nondominant hand for a one-handed C-E seal and mandible lift, and the other to squeeze. Switch to a two-person seal when possible.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How should crews combine BVM and spine motion restriction?
Choose a team position that preserves in-line stabilization, airway positioning, and an effective seal. The chapter illustrates manual stabilization and techniques at the head or side. Follow local practice.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What are the core BVM troubleshooting checks when the chest fails to rise?
Reposition, correct seal and size, check for obstruction, inspect bag assembly and oxygen flow, use an indicated adjunct, and switch method if ineffective.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What does visible abdominal distention during BVM suggest?
Gastric inflation from poor airway positioning, excessive volume, or fast breaths. Reposition and deliver slowly to visible chest rise.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is an ATV?
An automatic transport ventilator delivers preset rate and volume where device-specific use is authorized.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why might an EMS system use an ATV for prolonged support?
Preset ventilation can free both hands for the mask seal and airway positioning. Some devices have alarms, and lower inspiratory flow may reduce gastric inflation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What connector and portability examples does the chapter give for an ATV?
Standard 15/22-mm connector and a rugged device weighing 4 kg or less. Treat these as textbook equipment examples.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What limitations should an EMT consider before relying on a locally authorized ATV?
Oxygen-powered units stop when supply runs out, some models exclude children under 5, and the operator loses manual feedback on resistance and compliance.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What basic checks apply to a locally authorized ATV?
Verify function and oxygen supply, confirm seal and chest rise, monitor continuously, and keep a working BVM or pocket mask ready if it fails.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What may high- versus low-pressure alarms indicate on an authorized ATV?
High pressure can reflect resistance, kink, or poor lung compliance. Low pressure can reflect a leak or disconnect. Check ventilation and follow device-specific procedures.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How is PPV coordinated with spontaneous shallow breaths?
Explain and coach, then time assistance to the beginning of inhalation to augment tidal volume.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How does the chapter suggest transitioning a patient with markedly slow or rapid shallow breathing to supported breaths?
Start by synchronizing with spontaneous efforts, then adjust over several breaths. The textbook describes 5–10 assisted breaths for transition. Use current age- and context-specific rates.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What does CPAP stand for and how is it delivered?
Continuous positive airway pressure applies one continuous pressure during spontaneous breathing through a tightly sealed mask.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How can CPAP reduce work of breathing?
It recruits poorly aerated alveoli, can improve compliance, and splints airways open during expiration.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What does auto-PEEP mean in the chapter’s CPAP discussion?
Residual positive pressure from trapped air at the end of exhalation. Expiratory airway splinting can help reduce the work of breathing in selected patients.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How can CPAP help in cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
It recruits alveoli and can reduce left ventricular afterload and work of breathing.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Which conditions does the chapter discuss as possible indications for CPAP?
CHF or pulmonary edema, COPD, asthma, and pneumonia in selected patients, subject to local protocol and a compatible examination.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What general features make a patient a candidate for CPAP?
Awake and cooperative, protecting the airway, breathing spontaneously, adequately perfused, able to tolerate the mask, and without frequent suction needs or poor mask fit.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What do GCS, SBP, and RR stand for in BLS CPAP assessment?
Glasgow Coma Scale, systolic blood pressure, and respiratory rate.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Which numeric screening examples does the chapter give for CPAP?
Following commands with GCS above 10, RR above 25/min, SpO₂ below 94% or significant accessory muscle use, and often age over 12. Use local thresholds.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What are immediate reasons to avoid or stop CPAP?
Apnea or agonal breathing, arrest, loss of airway protection, unresponsiveness, active vomiting, severe hypotension, or inability to ventilate.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What other findings can make CPAP unsafe or unsuitable?
Suspected pneumothorax or chest trauma, facial injury or poor fit, upper GI bleeding or recent gastric surgery, tracheostomy, or frequent suction needs. Follow local contraindications.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What blood pressure cautions does the chapter give for CPAP?
Its examples list SBP below 90 mmHg as a contraindication and below 100 mmHg as a reason for consultation or adjustment. Use device-specific and local criteria.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How should an EMT prepare and position an authorized CPAP patient?
Explain, obtain baseline vitals and SpO₂, check equipment and backup oxygen, sit upright or at about 45° as tolerated, and secure a well-fitting, leak-free mask.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What pressures are used in the chapter’s CPAP example?
It describes a 4–20 cm H₂O range and illustrates starting at 5 cm H₂O with 2 cm H₂O increments up to a local maximum of 10 cm H₂O. Follow the device and local protocol.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How is a patient coached on CPAP in the chapter?
Reassure and coach inhalation through the nose and slow sustained exhalation through the mouth, illustrated with a slow count of four.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What reassessment interval and findings does the chapter give for CPAP?
Continuous SpO₂ with a vital-sign check about every 5 minutes in the example. Trend effort, mental status, air entry, heart rate, blood pressure, perfusion, and mask tolerance.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What oxygen and ventilation information should be reported when care is transferred?
Oxygen device and flow, saturation before and after oxygen, changes in effort and alertness, and any need for assisted ventilation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What response suggests CPAP is helping?
SpO₂ rises, breathing becomes easier, and respiratory rate, cyanosis, and accessory muscle use decrease while the patient remains alert and perfused.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why is a falling respiratory rate on CPAP sometimes concerning?
If alertness or effort declines too, the patient may be failing ventilation. Remove CPAP and provide appropriate BVM support.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why can a rising heart rate during CPAP accompany falling blood pressure?
Positive pressure can reduce venous return and preload. Check perfusion, blood pressure, and clinical response.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What complications should be monitored on CPAP?
Hypotension, pneumothorax, gastric distention, vomiting, worsening distress, declining alertness, and mask intolerance.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What should you do if an authorized CPAP patient loses airway protection or develops ineffective breathing?
Escalate immediately, remove CPAP, and provide indicated BVM support. Keep BVM and suction ready and notify the receiving team.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is the original chapter’s basic distinction between CPAP and BiPAP?
CPAP applies one constant pressure. Bilevel positive airway pressure applies higher pressure during inspiration and lower pressure during expiration.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is the BLS limitation of high-flow nasal oxygen in apnea or respiratory failure?
It can support oxygenation in selected patients but cannot substitute for effective assisted ventilation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How does excessive ventilation impair perfusion during cardiac arrest?
Sustained intrathoracic pressure decreases venous return and lowers coronary and cerebral blood flow.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How can overventilation reduce cardiac output in a spontaneously breathing patient?
Air trapping and lung overinflation compress pulmonary vessels and reduce venous return, preload and blood pressure.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: In the chapter case, a patient is unresponsive in vomit with a pulse and 6 shallow breaths/min. What should BLS prioritize?
Scene safety, coordinated repositioning as indicated, suction, manual airway opening, an OPA if gag is absent, effective oxygenated BVM, backup, and timely transport.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What upper-airway care did the crew provide before ventilating the patient found in vomit?
They rolled the patient supine with coordinated spine motion restriction, suctioned, used jaw thrust, and placed an OPA after finding no gag reflex. Actual spine motion restriction follows local policy.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What should you do if a ventilated patient vomits again during transport?
Clear the contamination promptly and resume effective ventilation. Recheck chest rise, vitals and oxygen delivery, and report recurrent contamination and aspiration risk.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What belongs in the handoff for a patient receiving ventilation after recurrent emesis?
Initial position and status, baseline and repeat vitals, trauma concerns, timing of emesis and suction, assisted chest rise, response, and need for ongoing ventilation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What equipment and documentation tasks follow the chapter’s recurrent-emesis transport case?
Give a verbal handoff, document assessments, interventions and responses in the patient care report, and clean and restock equipment.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: When should BLS request additional resources for an airway problem?
Early when deterioration or a difficult-to-maintain airway is likely. Coordinate rendezvous and destination under local policy while continuing indicated care and timely transport.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is a stoma in airway care?
A surgical neck opening into the trachea through which a patient may breathe.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is a tracheostomy and what does its tube do?
A surgical opening into the trachea, often with a curved hollow tube to keep it open. It may bypass upper obstruction or replace a long-standing oral tracheal tube.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How do airway routes differ after a tracheostomy versus total laryngectomy?
With tracheostomy, upper-airway continuity may remain and airflow may be split. After total laryngectomy, the mouth and nose are disconnected from the lungs and all air must pass through the stoma.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is a laryngectomy and how may a partial laryngectomy affect airflow?
Removal of all or part of the larynx. In the chapter’s partial example, some upper-airway connection remains and the patient may breathe through both the stoma and mouth or nose.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What should BLS do when a patient’s neck airway anatomy is uncertain?
Assess patency, give initial oxygen at face and stoma as indicated, and ask about surgery, airway route, baseline needs, airway card and emergency kit.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What suggests a blocked or displaced tracheostomy tube?
Absent airflow or inability to pass an authorized suction catheter. PPV through a displaced tube can inflate soft tissue.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How can a BVM interface with a patent tracheostomy tube?
Remove the face mask and attach the standard bag-valve connector directly to the compatible tube. When anatomy permits upward leakage, closing the mouth and nose may improve chest rise.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is the safety limit on switching to mouth-and-nose ventilation when a tracheostomy tube cannot be ventilated?
Consider a face route only when upper-airway continuity is possible and per protocol. Never use it to try to reach the lungs in a known total laryngectomy.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How should trained BLS personnel address secretions in a tracheostomy tube?
Use a soft suction catheter if authorized, following tube-specific and local instructions. Reassess airflow and suspect obstruction or displacement if patency fails.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What does the textbook illustrate for suction depth in an exposed stoma?
A sterile soft catheter with a 3–5 inch maximum in its example. Use applicable training and tube- or stoma-specific protocol. Do not advance to an arbitrary depth or force a catheter.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What positioning and mask does the chapter describe for BVM-to-stoma ventilation?
Expose and clear the stoma, keep the head straight and shoulders slightly raised, and use a small round or pediatric mask that seals over the opening.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What findings confirm effective BVM ventilation through a stoma?
Visible chest rise and fall and exhaled airflow returning through the stoma. Follow current protocol and use only enough volume for visible rise.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why might closing the mouth and nose improve stoma ventilation after a partial laryngectomy?
If an upper-airway connection remains, it may prevent gas from escaping upward.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What older BVM-to-stoma timing is described in the chapter, and how should it be used?
It illustrates a 2-second breath. Use current local BLS ventilation guidance and verify visible chest rise and exhalation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What points should BLS communicate after ventilating through a neck airway?
Which route produced chest rise, patency or suction problems, any suspected tube displacement, and changes from baseline.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is the preferred BLS alternative to direct mouth-to-stoma ventilation?
A BVM with a child- or infant-sized mask sealed over the stoma. If mouth-to-stoma is the only option, use a barrier.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What are the two major airway problems from facial trauma?
Soft-tissue swelling can occlude the airway and heavy pharyngeal bleeding may require repeated suction. Avoid NPA with midface trauma.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What does FBAO stand for?
Foreign-body airway obstruction.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How do you manage a responsive choking patient with an effective cough and air movement?
Encourage coughing, monitor for progression, and avoid thrusts while cough remains effective. Give oxygen if indicated and arrange transport as appropriate.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What indicates severe partial or complete FBAO in an adult?
Weak or silent cough, inability to speak or move air effectively, inspiratory stridor, and worsening labored breathing.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What sequence does the chapter’s 2025 AHA update specify for responsive adults with severe FBAO?
Alternate five back blows and five abdominal thrusts until relief or unresponsiveness.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: When do chest thrusts replace abdominal thrusts for a responsive adult with severe choking?
In late pregnancy or when the rescuer cannot encircle the abdomen.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What do you do when a patient with severe FBAO becomes unresponsive?
Start CPR with compressions, inspect for a visible object when opening the airway for breaths, and avoid blind sweeps. Apply the AED as soon as available when indicated.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What do you reassess immediately after relief of a foreign-body obstruction?
Breathing and pulse. With a pulse and ineffective breathing, provide PPV. If pulseless, start CPR and use an AED promptly.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What should persistent symptoms after FBAO relief raise concern for?
Residual obstruction or aspiration. Report the witnessed event, timing, cough, loss of responsiveness, and response to care.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What may partial obstruction look like in an infant or child?
An alert child may be pink or slightly pale with peripheral perfusion, and may cry or cough forcefully, with stridor, crowing, or retractions.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What clues suggest a foreign body in a child whose chest will not rise during PPV?
Continued resistance after repositioning, sudden choking or apnea near food or small objects, and no signs suggesting respiratory disease.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What causes of pediatric FBAO does the chapter highlight?
Liquids in infants and small objects, food, toys, or balloons in children.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why avoid manipulations for suspected epiglottitis?
A disease-related obstruction can worsen abruptly with mouth manipulation, causing swelling or spasm. Use FBAO maneuvers when the presentation supports a foreign body.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is mild FBAO care in an infant or child?
Allow effective coughing, monitor closely for worsening, and give indicated blow-by or supplemental oxygen per protocol. The textbook example targets SpO₂ at least 94%.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What sequence is used for a responsive infant younger than 1 year with severe FBAO?
Alternate five back blows and five chest thrusts using the heel of one hand per the chapter’s 2025 update.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How is the infant held during the two phases of severe choking care?
Support the head in a head-down position on the forearm, prone for back blows between the shoulder blades and supine for chest thrusts.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What sequence is used for a responsive child with severe FBAO?
Alternate five back blows and five abdominal thrusts until relief or unresponsiveness.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How does the chapter illustrate abdominal thrust placement in a responsive child?
Stand or kneel behind the child, place the thumb side of the fist between navel and xiphoid, grasp it, and thrust inward and upward. The thrusts are part of the updated alternating sequence.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Which infant CPR compression techniques supersede the textbook’s two-finger method?
Heel of one hand or two-thumb encircling hands in the chapter’s 2025 update.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What hand placement does the chapter show for compressions in an unresponsive child?
On the lower half of the sternum, with either one hand or two as appropriate to the child’s size. Begin with compressions per the current choking update.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Which older choking sequences does the chapter flag as superseded?
Adult or child thrust-only approaches, the adult three-cycle direction, and pediatric breath-first instructions after unresponsiveness.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What does SpO₂ estimate and what can affect the reading?
Peripheral hemoglobin oxygen saturation. Poor perfusion, motion, cold extremities, and skin pigmentation can affect accuracy.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How do you decide whether to trust a pulse oximeter reading?
Check signal quality and compare the displayed pulse and saturation with the actual pulse, perfusion, breathing, and clinical exam.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why can pulse oximetry be falsely reassuring in suspected CO exposure?
Standard two-wavelength oximetry can miss the reduction in usable oxygen carried by hemoglobin. Treat suspected carbon monoxide exposure with oxygen per protocol regardless of a reassuring reading.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What exposure details are useful at handoff after suspected CO poisoning?
Exposure setting, other symptomatic people, confusion or syncope, and known pregnancy.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Why is oxygen treated as a drug in BLS?
Choose indication, device, and concentration using clinical findings, reliable SpO₂, condition-specific targets, protocol, and medical direction.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Which general findings support supplemental oxygen when ventilation is adequate?
Hypoxemia, signs of hypoxia, or poor perfusion, interpreted with the condition and local protocol.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What are the chapter’s general medical oxygen trigger and target examples?
Signs of poor perfusion or shock, or SpO₂ below 94%, with a target at least 94% according to the example. Use condition-specific local guidelines.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How does the chapter’s general medical oxygen example escalate delivery?
Start nasal cannula at 2 L/min, titrate up to 6 L/min, and switch to nonrebreather at 10–15 L/min if the target is unmet.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What does the chapter’s trauma example recommend with major bleeding, shock, or poor perfusion?
High-concentration oxygen via nonrebreather at 10–15 L/min regardless of SpO₂, subject to local protocol.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What saturation triggers and guides oxygen in the chapter’s less severe trauma example?
Without major bleeding, shock or poor perfusion, SpO₂ below 95% triggers a nonrebreather at 10–15 L/min with a target above 95%. These are source examples.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What findings accompany the chapter’s older ACS oxygen trigger?
Dyspnea, hypoxemia, or overt signs of heart failure. Use the chapter’s updated hypoxemia qualification and local condition-specific protocol.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What do ACS, TBI, and COPD stand for?
Acute coronary syndrome, traumatic brain injury, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What is the chapter’s updated oxygen threshold in acute coronary syndrome?
Confirmed saturation below 90% supports oxygen. Routine oxygen at 90% or above is discouraged by the cited 2025 guideline.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How does the chapter illustrate titrating oxygen in hypoxemic ACS?
Start at 2 L/min by cannula, titrate up to 6 L/min and use a 10–15 L/min nonrebreather if the target is unmet. Its example targets at least 90%.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How should the chapter’s older stroke oxygen example be reconciled with its guideline update?
Its older example starts oxygen at 2 L/min when hypoxemia is suspected and targets at least 94%. The 2026 guidance cited by the chapter specifies above 94% in hypoxic ischemic stroke. Follow local policy and assess ventilation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What signs does the older stroke oxygen example use when deciding whether hypoxemia may be present?
SpO₂ below 94%, cyanosis, or unavailable saturation. Use the clinical exam and local protocol, including the chapter’s updated target if applicable.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: Which oxygen principle does the chapter cite for suspected severe TBI?
The severe TBI guidance cited in the chapter advises continuous supplementation and prompt correction of hypoxemia. Apply condition-specific prehospital protocols.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: How should the chapter’s blanket pregnancy oxygen rule be interpreted?
In maternal trauma or illness, assess breathing, oxygenation, perfusion, and exposure under local protocol. The older blanket rule for possible fetal hypoxia beyond 20 weeks does not replace that assessment, and routine oxygen for abnormal fetal heart patterns in normally oxygenated labor patients is discouraged in the cited intrapartum guidance.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What oxygen example does the chapter give for toxic inhalation?
Nonrebreather at 15 L/min regardless of saturation in the chapter example. Apply the relevant exposure protocol and reassess ventilation.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What saturation range is used for titrated oxygen in suspected COPD exacerbation in the chapter?
88–92% in the cited prehospital trial and textbook example, typically using a cannula. Apply local protocol and promptly correct hypoxemia.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: What should improving SpO₂ but worsening drowsiness or chest rise on oxygen prompt in COPD?
Immediately reassess ventilation. Report changes in effort, alertness, oxygen device and response, and assist ventilation if inadequate.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: In which chapter example would oxygen be unnecessary?
Isolated suspected ankle fracture with normal vitals, no hypoxia or poor perfusion, and 98% saturation on room air.

What does BLS stand for in EMS?: In the chapter’s MVC example, why does an adult with BP 102/88 mmHg, RR 22, SpO₂ 93%, and pale clammy skin warrant oxygen?
